text: The man lived among the tombs.
People had tried to help him, then feared him, then stayed away. He was alone in a place meant for the dead, crying out where no one wanted to go.
But Jesus crossed the water toward him. Help was already coming.
The man had been hurting for a long time. Evil had taken hold of him and torn his life apart. He couldn't live safely in his home or rest among his people.
Others had tried chains, but the chains didn't hold. They'd tried distance, but distance didn't heal him.
He needed more than strength against him. He needed authority over what held him.
Across the water, Jesus came with His disciples. The boat reached the shore, and the man saw Him. The evil inside the man knew Him too.
That changed everything.
The man ran toward Jesus.
It didn't look peaceful. It didn't look clean or easy. But the broken man was now standing before the only One who could truly free him.
The disciples watched, and the shore grew tense. The man wasn't too far gone.
Not for Jesus.
Jesus didn't run from him.
Others had feared the man. Others had kept away. Jesus stood before him with calm authority.
The evil spoke, but Jesus wasn't moved by it. He knew what was holding the man, and He had power over it.
The evil begged. That alone tells the story.
The man had been tormented for years, but the evil wasn't stronger than Jesus. It could rage in the man, frighten neighbors, and break chains. But it couldn't command the Son of God.
Jesus spoke, and the evil had to answer. The disciples saw the difference. The man wasn't facing a teacher only, or a helper only. He was facing the Lord, and the darkness knew it.
The evil had shouted long enough, and Jesus commanded it to leave. No battle of equals. No long struggle. No guessing.
Jesus spoke, and evil had to obey.
The change was terrible and sudden.
The evil left the man, and the scene broke open with force. Everyone nearby could see that something powerful had happened.
But the most important thing was the man. The one who'd been trapped was no longer trapped. The one who'd been driven was no longer driven.
Jesus had set him free.
When the people came, they saw the man sitting there.
That may have been the most shocking part. He wasn't running, crying out, fighting chains, or hiding among tombs.
He was sitting near Jesus, clothed, clear-minded, and free.
The people knew what he'd been. They knew the fear, the noise in the night, the shame around his name, and the way everyone had learned to avoid him.
Now they saw him changed. That should've made them rejoice. A son of their region had been restored, and a man who'd lived like the dead was alive in front of them.
But the people were afraid. Sometimes mercy frightens people when it comes with power they can't control.
They had wanted the man restrained. Jesus had made him whole. That was better, but it was also more than they knew how to handle.
So they asked Jesus to leave.
The healed man wanted to go with Jesus.
That made sense. Jesus had given him back his life. Anyone would want to stay close to the One who'd done that.
But Jesus gave him a different task. He told him to go home and tell what God had done for him.
The man had a story now, and his home needed to hear it.
The man left the tombs behind.
He walked toward home as a different man. The people who'd feared him would see him again, but not as before.
Jesus hadn't only freed him. Jesus had sent him.
The man didn't need a long sermon. He had his own life as proof. His family could look at him and see the mercy of God. His neighbors could hear his voice calm and clear.
That was enough.
He could say, "I was bound, and Jesus freed me." He could say, "I was lost among the tombs, and Jesus sent me home." He could say, "The evil had to obey Him."
No one could argue with the man standing in front of them. The story was simple, and it was strong.
Jesus had crossed the water for him. Jesus had spoken. The man was free.
The tombs weren't his home anymore.
Fear wasn't his name anymore, and evil didn't get the final word over his life. Jesus had the final word.
The man went back to his people with peace in his mind and mercy in his story.
He'd been alone among the dead. Now he was alive, and he was going home.
